newsitem.title: USA: Judge orders Detroit newspapers to rehire strikers.
newsitem.headline: Judge orders Detroit newspapers to rehire strikers.

text.p: A federal administrative law judge ordered Detroit's two newspapers to give 2,000 striking workers their jobs back after finding management committed unfair labour practices.

Judge Thomas Wilks, in a decision released Friday from the National Labour Relations Board in Washington, upheld most of the unfair labour practice complaints brought by the unions against the Detroit News and Detroit Free Press in the bitter, nearly two-year-old clash.
The unions hailed the decision as a victory, while the newspapers said they were likely to appeal the decision.
"Judge Wilks left no doubt about who the bad guys are in this dispute," Al Derey, chairman of the Metropolitan Council of Newspaper Unions, told cheering supporters at a news conference.

The decision means that the approximately 1,500 replacement reporters, distribution and production workers hired by the papers may be fired, if necessary, to make room for the returning strikers, Wilks said in his ruling.
Derey said the unions believe the NLRB will move quickly to seek a court order to enforce the reinstatement ruling.

Since the unions made an unconditional offer to return to work in February, only about 10 percent of the strikers have been rehired, he said. Union officials claim the papers could be responsible for up to $80 million a year in back pay if they refuse to take the workers back.

Wilks' decision upholds an earlier complaint from William Schaub, the regional NLRB director in Detroit, that the newspapers and their joint operating agency, Detroit Newspapers Inc., did not bargain in good faith with the six striking unions. Numerous other legal issues remain unresolved.

Included in Wilks' ruling is a finding that Detroit Newspapers violated a promise to bargain jointly with the unions and that the News imposed a merit pay on Newspaper Guild members without union permission.
The News is owned by Gannett Co. Inc., while Knight-Ridder Inc. owns the Free Press. The papers are editorially independent but jointly published by Detroit Newspapers.

Because of advance planning and tight security measures, the papers have published every day since the strike began on July 13, 1995. The walkout is regarded as one of the longest newspaper strikes to hit a major metropolitan area.

The newspapers said their attorneys were reviewing the 120-page opinion and were likely to appeal to the NLRB. If that fails, the papers can take their case to the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals and the U.S. Supreme Court, a process that analysts have said could take years.
Detroit Newspapers Chief Executive Officer Frank Vega called Wilks' ruling a split decision because he found against the unions on some matters.
"The decision is no surprise. We did not expect to win the entire case at this level, particulary before a judge appointed by the Labour Board," he said.
Since the sometimes-violent strike began, more than 400 strikers have returned to work, while others have left for other jobs. The papers said they had eliminated about 600 jobs through efficiencies.

Although they have continued to publish, the papers have said they lost $120 million in 1995 and 1996 due to the strike, circulation fell 30 percent and advertising was down 15 percent to 20 percent as of February.
Gannett stock dipped 75 cents to $97.75 Friday and Knight-Ridder fell 50 cents to $46.75, both in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
